newsitem.title: INDIA: India-Pakistan talks a chance to break trade jinx.
newsitem.headline: India-Pakistan talks a chance to break trade jinx.

text.p: Rare talks this week between India and arch-rival Pakistan offer an opportunity to tap vast South Asian trade potential long overshadowed by uneasy political relations, analysts said on Thursday.
The top-level diplomatic talks beginning on Friday between the two nations, stalled for nearly three years, could focus on easing trade barriers to spur economic growth, they said.

"The best way is to come economically closer and put the political problems on the back burner," said V. Raghuraman, secretary-general of India's Associated Chambers of Commerce of Industry (Assocham).

Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government, which came to power last month, has not spelled out its position on trade with India. But Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan tied it to progress on the territorial dispute over Kashmir.
"The possibility is there for trade, commerce, culture, but until you solve this particular issue (Kashmir), there will always be impediments," Khan told reporters earlier this month.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over Kashmir, since their independence from Britain in 1947.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has said that New Delhi and Islamabad should move ahead on trade issues to boost both of their economies.
Indian industry officials said Pakistan's economic troubles and India's economic growth were now pushing the two closer.
"Progress on trade between the two nations can bring about a minor, but significant, thaw," Indian political analyst Rashid Talib said. "It is a good time for us to press on trade issues."

Two-way trade between India and Pakistan in 1995/96 (April-March) increased to 4.07 billion rupees ($114 million) from 3.45 billion ($97 million) in the previous year, according to a study by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) that quoted official data.
"But the bulk of trade is done informally, mainly through third countries," said FICCI Secretary-general Amit Mitra.
Mitra said a FICCI study estimated that $1.0 billion in trade between India and Pakistan was routed through third countries and was not counted under bilateral trade.
Both India and Pakistan would benefit if trade between the two nations was liberalised, Mitra said.
"This is a win-win solution. Transaction costs will be lower for both the nations. The governments will also gain revenues."
Pakistani officials say problems over non-tariff barriers, quota restrictions and tariff cuts must be resolved by business leaders before the governments can make final decisions on them.
Pakistani business officials say they favour free trade with India in general, but want protection for some industries seen as vulnerable to Indian competition.
"We can start gradually in a phased manner," Ilyas Ahmed Bilour, president of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI), said in December.
The FPCCI and FICCI have agreed to set up an expert panel to suggest to their respective governments ways to boost trade between the two nations.

Thorny bilateral ties have cast a shadow over efforts by the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) nations -- Bhutan, Nepal, Maldives, Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan -- to form a free trade bloc, Raghuraman said.
Although New Delhi has already granted Pakistan a most favoured nation (MFN) trading status identical to that extended to other SAARC countries, Pakistan has failed to reciprocate.
